strengths: The benchmark targets an important problem: rapid saturation of visual-reasoning evaluations. Its 100 main questions require precise, multi-step reasoning rather than multiple-choice guessing, and the 334 subquestions provide some diagnostic signal when main-question accuracy is near zero.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a benchmark paper, covering 20 proprietary and open-weight LMMs, including reasoning models, with greedy pass@1, stochastic pass@5, and 5/5 reliability results (Table 2).

The construction process is clearly described: more than 20 creators produced 140 candidates, followed by independent review, refinement, and adversarial filtering. The inclusion of a benchmark canary is also a useful contamination precaution.

The paper reports model versions, prompts, decoding parameters, access dates, compute setup, completion-token usage, and approximate costs. These details improve reproducibility of the baseline evaluation, subject to proprietary API limitations.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. Examples in Figures 3 and 6 make the task structure understandable, while the appendix provides visually compelling examples of failures involving counting, spatial localization, reflections, diagrams, and simulated environments.

The contribution has practical significance: a compact benchmark is relatively inexpensive to run and is compatible with test-time-compute evaluations that would be costly on much larger suites. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The headline 0% result is largely guaranteed by construction rather than independently demonstrated: Section 3.1 explicitly removes every candidate answered correctly by any evaluated model, and essentially the same models are then used in Table 2 to establish that the benchmark is “impossible.” There is no held-out model set or held-out question-construction process, so the result does not establish that the procedure produces generally difficult questions rather than examples overfit to this particular model panel.

The paper supplies no human baseline or systematic validation that questions are unambiguous and reliably answerable from the provided images. Statements that the benchmark is “high-quality and noise-free” rest on internal review, without reporting annotator counts per item, independent solution rates, agreement, expert qualifications, or adjudication outcomes. This is especially concerning for intricate questions involving tiny visual details and bespoke conventions.

The claimed error analysis is not rigorous enough to support its conclusions. Section 5.3 says errors are “heavily skewed” toward visual interpretation rather than reasoning or knowledge, but provides no annotation protocol, category definitions, number of responses labeled, inter-rater agreement, or quantitative distribution. Figures 7–13 are selected qualitative examples, predominantly from o1 pro, and cannot establish a cross-model prevalence claim.

Exact-match scoring is under-specified for a heterogeneous open-ended benchmark. The paper does not explain normalization, accepted equivalent forms, units, numerical tolerances, ordering variants, or manual adjudication. Moreover, o1 pro and QVQ are parsed and judged using Gemini 2 Flash whereas other models are evaluated by direct parsing, introducing an inconsistent evaluator whose accuracy is not validated.

The benchmark’s diagnostic resolution remains limited. All models tie at 0% under the primary deterministic metric, while pass@5 reaches 7%, contradicting the strongest literal framing of complete impossibility. Subquestions distinguish models, but they are manually derived, vary in number by main question, and are macro-averaged by parent question; the paper does not analyze their difficulty, dependencies, or whether they validly measure the same capabilities as the main tasks.

Statistical treatment is incomplete. A sample of 100 questions gives substantial uncertainty even for an observed zero accuracy, yet no confidence bound is reported for main-question performance. The reported CLT standard errors for subquestions do not address adversarial selection, heterogeneous task difficulty, correlated subquestions, or uncertainty from stochastic decoding.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript states that the dataset will be publicly released, but the abstract contains no usable repository link, and the paper itself does not provide the complete questions, images, annotations, acceptable-answer rules, evaluation code, model outputs, or error labels. Proprietary APIs and the semi-automated ChatGPT evaluation of o1 pro further prevent exact replication.

For an ICML 2026 submission, the empirical model panel is stale: API access occurred January 27–30, 2025. The manuscript therefore does not substantiate its repeated claims about “contemporary” or future frontier models at the time of review. Evaluation on current models, preferably excluded from benchmark selection, is essential.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Hand-crafting difficult multimodal questions, decomposing them into subquestions, and adversarially filtering against frontier models are useful in combination, but each has close precedents acknowledged by the paper. Without independent validity evidence, the main novelty risks reducing to selecting a set on which the chosen systems scored zero.

strengths: The paper targets a real evaluation problem: many multimodal benchmarks are rapidly saturating, while expensive test-time reasoning makes compact evaluations attractive.
The benchmark contains bespoke, open-ended, multi-step questions spanning natural and synthetic images, rather than relying mainly on multiple-choice items that permit guessing.
The empirical coverage is broad: 20 proprietary and open-weight LMMs are evaluated, with pass@1, pass@5, 5/5 reliability, completion-token costs, and 334 diagnostic subquestions.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The construction pipeline, prompt, model versions, inference dates, and most decoding settings are documented, which provides a useful foundation for reproducibility.
The qualitative examples expose recognizable weaknesses in counting, fine-detail perception, spatial interpretation, reflection, diagram tracing, and state simulation.
weaknesses: Soundness: the headline result is largely guaranteed by construction. The authors test candidate questions on the baseline models and delete every item answered correctly by any model, then evaluate those same models on the retained set. Consequently, universal 0% pass@1 is an in-sample selection outcome rather than independent evidence that the benchmark is intrinsically 'impossible' or that it validly measures general visual reasoning.

Soundness: there is no reported human baseline, expert-performance estimate, response-time study, or inter-annotator agreement. The assertion that all questions are answerable, unambiguous, correctly labeled, and 'noise-free' rests on internal review, with no quantitative validation. This is especially concerning for intricate questions involving image measurements, counting, specialized knowledge, or multi-step exact answers.

Significance: the main-question metric cannot distinguish any of the 20 contemporary systems. The subquestions provide some separation, but their validity as decompositions of the intended reasoning processes is not established. A benchmark deliberately optimized to collapse current systems to zero offers limited present-day diagnostic value, and its future ranking validity is speculative.

The benchmark conflates several sources of failure—visual perception, resolution limits, OCR, domain knowledge, long compositional reasoning, and exact-output formatting—without a taxonomy or controlled subsets. The authors explicitly decline to categorize questions, weakening interpretability and making aggregate progress difficult to diagnose.

The claimed error analysis is not rigorous enough to support its central conclusion that visual interpretation, rather than reasoning, is the dominant failure source. No annotation protocol, category counts, annotator agreement, uncertainty analysis, or complete quantitative results are given; a handful of selected examples cannot establish prevalence or comparisons with prior work.

Evaluation is brittle and inconsistent. Most responses are scored by exact string matching, while outputs from o1 pro and QVQ are parsed and judged using Gemini 2 Flash. The paper does not report normalization rules, judge validation, disagreement rates, or manual audits, so semantically equivalent answers may be treated differently across models.

The construction procedure introduces further adaptive bias: creators repeatedly queried frontier models, altered questions to increase difficulty, refined the prompt during experimentation, and adversarially filtered on the final baseline family. No held-out question pool or held-out model study is provided to estimate generalization beyond this adaptive process.

Statistical treatment is limited. Only standard errors for subquestion averages are shown; there are no uncertainty intervals or paired significance tests for model comparisons. Subquestions are clustered within main questions, vary in number and dependence, and are manually selected, making the reported hierarchy difficult to interpret. Pass@5 estimates based on only five samples are also noisy.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. Hand-crafted hard multimodal evaluation and adversarial filtering are established ideas; the main novelty is pushing filtering until all selected models score zero. The manuscript does not demonstrate that this design yields better validity, longevity, or scientific insight than retaining a calibrated range of difficulties.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite good reporting of model versions and settings. Proprietary models, o1 pro's ChatGPT-interface defaults, semi-automated collection, API drift, and model-specific multi-image handling prevent faithful replication. The manuscript also does not fully specify the benchmark's answer-normalization and evaluator implementation.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. The future-outlook section acknowledges resolution constraints and selection effects for new models, but there is no focused discussion of adaptive overfitting, human validity, exact-match bias, image provenance/licensing, privacy, or accessibility. The generic impact statement does not address these benchmark-specific concerns.

strengths: Significance: ZeroBench addresses a real evaluation problem—rapid saturation of multimodal benchmarks—and its lightweight design is particularly useful when evaluating expensive test-time-reasoning models.

Soundness: The benchmark construction is unusually deliberate: more than 20 creators produced 140 candidates, non-creator review reduced these to 106, and adversarial filtering produced 100 difficult main questions. The 334 associated subquestions recover useful signal despite the floor on main-question accuracy.

Evaluation breadth is strong, covering 20 proprietary and open-weight LMMs, including reasoning models. Model versions, access dates, prompts, decoding parameters, token usage, pass@5, and 5/5 reliability are reported.

The results reveal a practically relevant gap between stochastic success and reliability: Gemini 2 Flash Thinking reaches 7% pass@5, yet every model remains at 0% under 5/5 reliability. Subquestion scores also differentiate systems, ranging from 3.38% to 24.30%.

Originality is moderate but meaningful. Adversarial benchmark filtering is established, but combining extremely difficult bespoke visual tasks, lightweight evaluation, explicit subproblem decomposition, and reliability measurements provides a useful new resource.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The paper motivates its design choices well, provides concrete question and failure examples, and candidly acknowledges that unseen models may obtain nonzero scores without necessarily being more capable.
weaknesses: The headline 0% result is circular: the final questions are precisely those that none of the evaluated models answered correctly during adversarial filtering, after candidate questions were also tailored using frontier models. Re-evaluating essentially the same model pool cannot independently establish that the benchmark is broadly “impossible for contemporary LMMs.” A held-out model set or later model snapshot is needed.

The main metric has no discriminative value among the tested models, while the informative subquestions constitute a related but materially easier evaluation. Their number and difficulty vary across main questions, and the paper provides no principled validation that the macro-averaged subquestion score measures a consistent construct.

The asserted high quality and answerability are insufficiently demonstrated. There is no human baseline, independent solver study, inter-annotator agreement, or detailed adjudication report. These checks are especially important for bespoke questions involving ambiguous real images, specialized knowledge, or exact multi-step calculations.

The claim that failures are primarily visual rather than reasoning-based is supported only by selected qualitative examples. No error taxonomy, annotation protocol, category counts, uncertainty, or annotator agreement is reported, despite the paper describing the analysis as rigorous.

Exact-match evaluation is brittle for open-ended answers with equivalent formats, units, rounding, or wording. Moreover, QVQ and o1 pro use Gemini 2 Flash for parsing and comparison, but the accuracy of this exceptional judging pipeline is not audited.

Input treatment is not fully controlled: some multi-image questions are supplied as separate images, whereas vLLM-hosted models and Llama 3.2 receive collages. Provider-specific image resizing further confounds comparisons, particularly because the paper argues that fine detail and resolution drive many failures.

Reproducibility is mixed. Prompts, model identifiers, dates, and most hyperparameters are documented, but proprietary endpoints may not remain reproducible, o1 pro is evaluated through a semi-automated interface, and the manuscript does not provide an accessible release link, complete annotations, or evaluation code. The benchmark’s small public test set is also highly vulnerable to future contamination despite the canary string.

The abstract’s statement that all models score 0.0% is potentially misleading without specifying greedy pass@1, since stochastic pass@5 reaches 7%. The generic impact statement also omits image provenance, licensing, privacy, and consent considerations for the 69 natural-image questions.
